exports.4: We have a lake that began as a swampy river arm nobody would swim in until somebody closed one end with rubble, and it is now the best thing we own. Send us the levels for the low end of Market Street and we'll send back three drainage engineers, a truck of interlocking concrete units and a plan that stops apologising for the water: dig the low point deeper, line it, put steps down one side, and by the second summer rent out a pedalo.
exports.5: Fame isn't a recipe, it's a smell that reaches the end of the street by four in the afternoon. We'll lend you two grill men and their scarred iron plates for a season to establish one dish and one dish only — lamb and onion pressed into hot flatbread, eaten standing, no cutlery, stall opens at four and closes when the meat runs out — and the queue will do the rest of the advertising.
exports.8: Do not build a wall. We built the wall, and a solid one just carries the problem forty metres further down and makes it meaner on arrival. Our precast yard can ship perforated concrete screens, roughly forty percent open, set staggered and angled down both sides of the avenue: they bleed the speed out of it instead of arguing with it, they take planters along the base, and the holes hum in a gale, which after one winter people start defending to visitors.
exports.9: Put nothing scenic on the far side. Half of our city sits on a mud flat that nobody crossed to for twenty years, and what finally moved people was not a view, it was the bus depot and the green market — so gut the appliance showroom, put the produce market inside it with the fish stalls against the back wall so everyone has to walk the full length, and we'll send our market cooperative's stall layout plus two licensing clerks to run the first six months for you.
exports.10: Your studies are counting spaces and your residents are counting the minutes they spend with the indicator on, and those are different quantities, so both sides can keep being right forever. Borrow forty of the men who stand on our corners waving cars into gaps you would swear were not there — put them in a vest, pay them a wage instead of a coin, one per contested block; the arithmetic doesn't move an inch, but nobody circles alone any more and the grievance quietly loses its object.
exports.11: Our street trees stand in salt every winter because we grit like lunatics, and the survivors are always the same three: tamarisk, sea buckthorn and an ugly hybrid poplar nobody has ever photographed. Take cuttings from our depot by the crate, plant them in raised beds with a coarse gravel layer underneath so rain flushes the salt down past the roots rather than parking it there, and accept that the promenade will look scruffy for six years and then be a windbreak.
exports.12: We ran shift nurseries beside the plants for forty years and three of them still take children at eleven at night, and the thing nobody expects is that a night room is not a day room with the lights off — it is beds, one waking adult per six sleeping children, a bath at handover and breakfast at 6:15 so the parent eats too. We'll send the rota, the staffing ratios and the retired matron who wrote both, on the single condition that the employers pay for it and not the grandmothers.
exports.13: A rival from overseas is a friendly with extra travel. The ones that work live twenty minutes away and use the same butcher — so split the club: give the half of the town on the wrong side of the harbour road the older kit, the worse pitch and a grievance about a disputed goal in 1974 that we will happily draft in convincing detail, and we'll send two veterans of our supporters' club for a fortnight to teach the drumming, the banners and exactly where the line sits.
exports.15: Ours open at four, and the rule of the house is that nobody serving asks how the night went. Feed them hot and without ceremony — flaky cheese pastry cut and sold by weight, soup with a bone actually in it, one small brandy that is nobody's business at that hour, coffee strong enough to stand a spoon in — and keep one long table reserved for them, away from the window, so the eight o'clock people cannot sit there and describe their commute.

answers.4: Against, and for the record it is chemistry, not taste. It comes at me like the inside of a new plastic bucket, and I'm told that reaction is genetic, which I choose to read as science taking my side rather than excusing me.
answers.5: The tin ashtray from the kafana on my corner, which shut in March. Everybody took something that last night and I took that, and somebody in fifty years ought to know a room like that existed and roughly what it smelled like.
answers.7: Same table, outside if the weather permits any argument at all, from about seven. One coffee that lasts ninety minutes, then something with an opinion in it. Three people — four and it turns into a meeting, and I have meetings. The argument has to be about something with no consequences whatsoever: a referee, a bridge, whether the old bus route was better before they straightened it. Then I walk home along the water at eleven, on my own, and I don't look at the phone until I'm through the door.
answers.9: My sister. Not because she'll be pleased — she'll have found the flaw in it inside a minute — but because if it gets past her it's real.
answers.10: Somewhere two rivers meet. I couldn't settle in a place with only one, it would feel like a town that gave up halfway. Novi Sad, probably, and I would complain about it daily and stay thirty years.
answers.11: A twelve-kilo lump of concrete off the old bridge parapet, handed to me as a joke when they replaced the span. It holds down nothing, it has scratched the desk in four places, and it is the only object in the room anyone ever asks about.
answers.12: If they're truly equal I take whichever one is easier to undo. And if they're equally easy to undo, I take the one that irritates the loudest person in the room, because then at least by Thursday we've learned something.
answers.13: The kitchen. Eighth floor, concrete block, new part of town. There was a balcony off it that my father glazed in badly over one weekend, so it cooked in July and was no use at all in January, and that's where the onions and the jars of pickle lived. The table was too big for the room and shoved against the wall, and you had to go sideways past it to reach the fridge. Everything happened in there — homework, arguments, my grandmother's card game, the radio left on for the football. My own bedroom I remember almost nothing about.
answers.14: There's a bench at the end of a pier that only the fishermen use, and none of them speak to anybody before noon. I take a coffee down and sit at the wrong end of it.
answers.16: A key to a flat I haven't lived in since 1998, which has certainly had the lock changed twice. It's on my keyring. It's staying on my keyring.
